title: Potential Errors When Performing Tests
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 3.8 Potential Errors When Performing Tests
intro: After this lesson you can describe Type I and Type II errors in context with their consequences, state their probabilities, define power, and explain what increases the power of a test.

moments.title: A correct test can still reach a wrong conclusion
moments.text: The error is not in the work. The sample evidence can point to the wrong decision about the population.

moments.title: Defective chairs
moments.text: A company tests $H_0: p=0.04$ against $H_a: p>0.04$ with 300 chairs at the 5% level.

moments.title: Reject $H_0$ can mean a Type I error
moments.text: With a p-value of 0.023, the test rejects $H_0$. If $H_0$ is actually true, that is a Type I error.

moments.title: Type I error
moments.text: There is convincing evidence for $H_a$, but $H_a$ is not true.

moments.title: Consequence of a Type I error
moments.text: The company stops production and pays for repairs it does not need.

moments.title: Fail to reject can mean a Type II error
moments.text: With a p-value of 0.068, the test fails to reject $H_0$. If $H_a$ is actually true, that is a Type II error.

moments.title: Type II error
moments.text: There is not convincing evidence for $H_a$, but $H_a$ is true.

moments.title: Consequence of a Type II error
moments.text: The company keeps producing too many defective chairs.

moments.title: Power
moments.text: The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis.

moments.title: $P(\text{Type I})=\alpha$
moments.text: The significance level is the probability of a Type I error.

moments.title: $P(\text{Type II})=1-\text{power}$
moments.text: Called $\beta$ in the video. Power and the Type II error probability add to 1.

moments.title: Raise $\alpha$ to raise power
moments.text: A larger rejection region makes rejection easier, but the Type I error probability rises too.

moments.title: Increase the sample size
moments.text: A larger $n$ lowers the standard error, so true differences stand out.

moments.title: Larger true difference, more power
moments.text: A true proportion of 18% is far easier to detect than 5.3% when the claim is 4%.

moments.title: After-school tutoring
moments.text: $H_0: p=0.70$ against $H_a: p<0.70$. Describe both errors and their consequences.

moments.title: Always include the consequence
moments.text: Name the error, state what is true, state the conclusion reached, then the consequence.

cards.name: Type I
cards.text: You reject $H_0$. Possible error: $H_0$ was actually true.

cards.name: Type II
cards.text: You fail to reject $H_0$. Possible error: $H_a$ was actually true.

cards.name: No error
cards.text: The conclusion matches the truth. Rejecting a false $H_0$ is power.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: You can never know whether you made an error. Say "might" when linking a conclusion to an error, and describe the error as what would be true, not as something you know happened.

sections.title: Describe an error and raise power

questions.obj: Describe Type I and Type II errors in context
questions.q: A company thinks more than 4% of its chairs are defective. It tests whether the proportion is greater than 0.04 using a sample of 300 chairs. Describe a Type I error and a Type II error in context and state a consequence of each.

work.text: Here $p$ is the proportion of all chairs the company produces that are defective.

steps.t: Type I error: say what is true and what the test concludes.

work.text: The true proportion of defective chairs is 0.04 or less, but the test finds convincing evidence that it is more than 0.04. The null hypothesis is true, and the test rejects it.

steps.t: Type II error: say what is true and what the test concludes.

work.text: The true proportion of defective chairs is more than 0.04, but the test does not find convincing evidence of this. The alternative hypothesis is true, and the test fails to reject the null.

steps.t: State a consequence of each error.

work.text: After a Type I error the company stops production and pays for repairs it does not need. After a Type II error it keeps producing too many defective chairs.

questions.answer: Type I: the true proportion of defective chairs is 0.04 or less, but the test finds convincing evidence that it is more than 0.04, so the company wastes time and money fixing a problem that does not exist. Type II: the true proportion is more than 0.04, but the test does not find convincing evidence of it, so the company keeps making too many defective chairs.

questions.obj: Describe both errors when the alternative is a lower tail
questions.q: An administrator thinks fewer than 70% of students in an after-school tutoring program improve their math grade. If the proportion is lower, he will cut the program. He tests whether the proportion is less than 0.70. Describe a Type I error and a Type II error in context and state a consequence of each.

work.text: Here $p$ is the proportion of students in the program who improve their math grade.

steps.t: Type I error: say what is true and what the test concludes.

work.text: The true proportion who improve is 0.70 or more, but the test finds convincing evidence that it is less than 0.70.

steps.t: Type II error: say what is true and what the test concludes.

work.text: The true proportion who improve is less than 0.70, but the test does not find convincing evidence of this.

steps.t: State a consequence of each error.

work.text: After a Type I error the administrator cuts a program that works. After a Type II error he keeps a program that is not working well enough.

questions.answer: Type I: the true proportion who improve is 0.70 or more, but the test finds convincing evidence that it is less than 0.70, so the administrator cuts a program that works. Type II: the true proportion is less than 0.70, but the test does not find convincing evidence of it, so the program that is not working well enough is kept.

questions.obj: Explain how to increase the power of a test
questions.q: For the chair test of $H_0:p=0.04$ against $H_a:p>0.04$ at $\alpha=0.05$ with $n=300$, the true proportion is 0.053. Describe three ways to increase power and give a drawback of one of them.

work.text: A larger sample lowers the standard error, so a small true difference is easier to see.
A larger rejection region makes rejection easier when the alternative is true.

steps.t: Note that a true value farther from $p_0$ gives more power.

work.text: You cannot choose the truth, but a true proportion of 0.18 is much easier to detect than 0.053.
Raising $\alpha$ raises the probability of a Type I error as well as power.

questions.answer: Power increases with a larger sample size, a larger significance level, or a true value farther from the null value. Raising the significance level also raises the probability of a Type I error.

buttons.label: Watch the three ways to raise power (12:09)

traps.title: Type I error in context with a consequence
traps.weak: A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis.
traps.better: A Type I error: the true proportion of students who improve is 0.70 or more, but the test finds convincing evidence that it is below 0.70. The principal cuts a program that works.

traps.title: Type II error in context with a consequence
traps.weak: A Type II error is failing to reject the null when it is false.
traps.better: A Type II error: the true proportion who improve is below 0.70, but the test does not find convincing evidence of this. The school keeps a program that is not working well enough.

traps.title: Calling an error a calculation mistake
traps.weak: A Type I error means the statistician made a math mistake.
traps.better: A Type I or Type II error is a wrong conclusion that can happen even when all the work is correct, because samples vary.

traps.title: Saying alpha is the chance the null is true
traps.weak: $\alpha=0.05$ means a 5% chance that $H_0$ is true.
traps.better: $\alpha=0.05$ is the probability of rejecting $H_0$ when $H_0$ is true, that is, the Type I error probability.

traps.title: Raising alpha with no cost
traps.weak: Raising $\alpha$ to 0.10 only helps because power rises.
traps.better: Raising $\alpha$ raises power but also raises the probability of a Type I error.

questions.stem: A test of $H_0: p=0.30$ against $H_a: p>0.30$ gives a p-value of 0.012 at $\alpha=0.05$. Which error is possible?
opts: Both Type I and Type II
why: Correct. The test rejects $H_0$, so the only possible error is a Type I error.
A Type II error requires failing to reject $H_0$.
Only one decision was made, so only one error is possible.
Any decision from a sample could be wrong.

questions.stem: Which change would increase the power of a test of one proportion, with everything else fixed?
opts: Choose a null value closer to the true proportion
why: A true value closer to $p_0$ is harder to detect and lowers power.
A smaller sample raises the standard error and lowers power.
A smaller $\alpha$ shrinks the rejection region and lowers power.
Correct. A larger sample lowers the standard error and raises power.

questions.stem: A test has power 0.82. What is the probability of a Type II error for the same alternative?
why: 0.05 would be a typical $\alpha$, not related to power.

questions.stem: A town tests $H_0: p=0.50$ against $H_a: p<0.50$ for support of a new bus route. Which is a Type II error in context?
opts: Concluding support is above 50% when it is below 50%
Concluding support is below 50% when it is actually 50% or more
Concluding there is not enough evidence that support is below 50% when it actually is below 50%
Concluding support is exactly 50% when it is 50%
why: The alternative is a lower tail, so this is not the opposite error.
This describes a Type I error.
Correct. A Type II error fails to reject a false $H_0$.

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: A city claims that at most 20% of its buses run late. A rider group suspects it is more than 20% and tests $H_0: p=0.20$ against $H_a: p>0.20$ at $\alpha=0.05$ using a random sample of buses.
parts: (a) Describe a Type I error in context and give a consequence.
(b) Describe a Type II error in context and give a consequence.
(c) What is the probability of a Type I error?
(d) The group wants a test with more power. Give two changes and state one drawback of one of them.
sample: (a) The true proportion of late buses is 0.20 (or less), but the test finds convincing evidence that it is more than 0.20. The city spends money to fix a problem that does not exist.
(b) The true proportion of late buses is greater than 0.20, but the test does not find convincing evidence of this. The city does nothing and riders keep facing late buses.
(d) Take a larger sample, or increase $\alpha$. Increasing $\alpha$ raises the probability of a Type I error.
checklist: (a) States the truth and the conclusion in context
(b) States the truth and the conclusion in context
(d) Names the drawback of a larger alpha
